top_evidence.document_title: A patient-centered approach to inclusive AI in healthcare: potential benefits, challenges, and recommendations
top_evidence.text: Several limitations should be considered when interpreting the results of this review. First, our selection of sources was mostly linked to publications that explored or contributed to 'inclusive AI'. Thus, there is a potential of omitting other relevant studies linked to patient-centered healthcare due to the terminologies used in the search strategy. Moreover, we did not include variations of these terms, additional keywords, or expand the search to the entire manuscript. As a result, relevant articles that used alternative terminology or did not explicitly include these keywords in the abstract may have been overlooked. Additionally, our search was limited to English-only databases and grey literature such as non-governmental reports on AI in low- and middle-income countries, which introduces a potential selection bias. However, the inclusion of articles published between 2020 and 2024 ensures that the review reflects the latest trends and developments in the field of inclusive AI in healthcare. Addi - tionally, although our search was comprehensive and used several databases, it was limited to publications indexed in established databases, which may have excluded relevant or recent works published in other platforms such as preprints or institutional repositories.

top_evidence.text: The search resulted in 1,377 results. After removing duplicates in EndNote and Rayyan, we kept 1,163 results for further screening. In the title and abstract screening, both reviewers agreed to exclude 1,124 references; 39 articles were considered appropriate to be screened in depth during full-text review. Twenty-one were excluded at this stage; the list of excluded articles during the full-text screening and the reason for their exclusion is presented in Appendix 2. A total of 18 articles were included in this review [1, 5, 6, 8, 9, 22-34] (see Fig. 1, and Table 1). All included articles were published between 2020 and 2024. top_evidence.section: Data Items And Data Extraction > Methods
top_evidence.text: All selected articles were included in qualitative synthesis and were divided between two authors (EG and KD), with each author extracting data from half of the articles. After which further discussion was carried out among the three authors during data extraction. The following information was extracted from each study: Healthcare context (e.g., condition, medical specialty); Type of AI solution (e.g., AI-based prediction algorithm, natural language processing, chatbot); Use of frameworks and/or guidelines to ensure inclusivity in AI; Specific methods for implementing inclusivity within the AI solution; and the discussed SWOT data addressing the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats of inclusive AI solutions. The classification of discussed topics into SWOT categories was based on the characteristics highlighted in each article. When the categorization was explicitly stated by the authors, it was directly adopted. When not clearly reported, positive characteristics already in place and described positively were classified as Strengths, while positive characteristics expected to occur were classified as Opportunities. Negative characteristics that have already occurred were classified as Weaknesses, and negative characteristics anticipated to occur were classified as Threats. These classifications were performed by the author responsible for extracting the data. In this study, a literature review was adopted as the chosen research approach by carrying out a systematic review with conceptual synthesis, following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines [21], as seen in Appendix 3. We searched six databases (PubMed, PsycINFO, CINAHL, Academic Search Premier, IEEE Xplore, and Scopus) for publications that included the keyword 'Inclusive AI' in their abstract. In this study we prioritize the literature to explicitly addressing 'inclusive AI' in healthcare as this area has not been well addressed in prior studies. Accordingly, we used only the keyword 'Inclusive AI' 'strategies', 'solutions', 'regulatory frameworks', 'applications', 'benefits', 'challenges', AND 'bias', 'fair - ness', 'equity', OR 'diversity' AND 'healthcare' to ensure the search captured publications where inclusivity was an explicit and central focus. The search was conducted on the 26th of September 2024. The search was carried out again on the 16th of April 2026 after extending the search keyword based on the research questions being examined in this study to improve the literature. The full search strategy can be found in Appendix 1. We uploaded all identified refer - ences to EndNote, removed duplicates, and then uploaded the remaining references to Rayyan.

top_evidence.section: Critical Appraisal Of The Included Articles
top_evidence.text: All 17 expert opinion articles met the JBI Checklist criteria for expert opinion, with unanimous 'Yes' ratings across the first five domains: clear identification of the opinion source, author standing in the field of expertise, central focus on the interests of the relevant population (marginalized, racial, and ethnic minorities in AI-health contexts), logically defended arguments supporting the conclusions drawn, and comprehensive reference to the extant literature (See Table 2). For the sixth domain, 10 articles reported no significant incongruence with existing sources, while the remaining seven explicitly acknowledged and logically defended noted incongruences, including the dominance of high-income country perspectives requiring adaptation to low- and middle-income settings, the integration of nonWestern ethical frameworks such as Ubuntu, the limitations of individual-responsibility models in distributed AI systems, gaps in the literature, the generally optimistic framing of AI and AgeTech, and author's optimism despite current harms associated with AI literature (See Table 2). Using PROBAST, the study of Ekellem et al. [28] was judged to have a high risk of bias across specially in the analysis domain due to overfitting, lack of proper validation, and small sample size. Additional concerns were identified in participant selection and outcome definition, limiting the generalizability and reliability of the findings (See Table 3).

top_evidence.document_title: A patient-centered approach to inclusive AI in healthcare: potential benefits, challenges, and recommendations
top_evidence.text: Many AI models inherit biases due to the underrepresentation of diverse populations in datasets and reliance on historically biased data. This leads to unfair and less inclusive outcomes. Aspects contributing to these weaknesses mentioned in the papers are lack of diverse data, over-reliance on datasets from high-income countries or bias in clinical care. Another weakness is the lack of standardized frameworks, ethical guidelines, and clear user consent processes. This hinders AI adoption by mistrust and concerns about fairness. AI decision-making is often a 'black box,' making it difficult to understand and correct biases. Lack of user input integration further limits inclusivity. AI systems can perpetuate cultural insensitivity, breach privacy, and lead to excessive dependence on technology for essential decision-making. Disparities in access to AI-driven tools such as accessibility barriers or limited adoption in low-resource areas create gaps in inclusivity, particularly for underserved populations. The most frequently mentioned weaknesses were bias and data limitations, cited in 16 articles, emphasizing how underrepresentation in datasets and reliance on biased historical data limit inclusivity and fairness [1, 5, 6, 8, 9, 22, 23, 25-31, 33, 34]. A total of 18 articles were included in this literature review, all published between 2020 and 2024. The critical appraisal indicated that the majority of articles included were expert opinion papers meeting key JBI quality criteria, suggesting a generally strong conceptual and theoretical foundation. However, the predominance of expert opinion highlights a limited availability of empirical evidence in the field of inclusive AI in healthcare. These articles focused on AI applications in health, including general healthcare, cancer care, mental health, and specific conditions like cogni - tive disabilities. These articles referred to various AI types, including machine learning, chatbots, and convolutional neural networks. Multiple frameworks for ensuring inclusive AI were reported, such as ACCEPT-AI, Bias Mitigation, and human rights values frameworks. However, some articles did not mention specific inclusivity frameworks. The SWOT analysis highlights improved accessibility and inclusivity as a key strength, while the most frequently identified weakness is bias and data limitations. Among the opportunities, advancing health equity and fostering innovation in design, frameworks, and policy were the most discussed topics. The most commonly cited threat was the potential for AI to exacerbate inequities, excluding some race, certain gender, thereby widening health disparities. We identified several recurring themes related to the participatory health approach that AI technologies are supporting. These themes center on empowering patients, improving communication and relationships, promoting shared decision-making, and fostering equitable healthcare practices. These application areas support the need to design AI technologies inclusively in order not to exclude individuals from benefiting from healthcare services delivered by AI technologies [4]. We also identified several opportunities for inclusive AI. Inclusive AI can play a transformative role in reducing healthcare and digital inequities by improving access for marginalized populations and addressing social determinants of health. By applying inclusive design frameworks, considering regulatory frameworks and participatory approaches during the development, inclusive AI can foster trust and transparency of AI solutions. Co-design methodologies and international collaborations in aggregating data sets to be used in AI systems may improve AI fairness. Educating stakeholders on AI applications and limitations can improve adoption and reduce skepticism. AI can improve in accuracy and personalization by refining models, improving data collection, and leveraging privacy-preserving learning techniques. Among opportunities, we identified two big topics as the most commonly discussed: the potential in advancing health equity and innovations in design [5, 9, 22, 24, 27, 28, 30, 33] and the need of inclusive frameworks and policy [1, 6, 8, 25, 27, 28, 31, 32], each discussed in 8 articles.

top_evidence.document_title: A patient-centered approach to inclusive AI in healthcare: potential benefits, challenges, and recommendations
top_evidence.text: From the results, we derived facets of inclusive AI solutions in healthcare, formulated recommendations addressing these facets to achieve inclusive AI in healthcare and formulated a research agenda. In order to assess eligibility, two authors (EG and KD) independently screened the titles and abstracts of all identified articles. In the second step, two authors (EG and AJB) independently assessed the eligibility of the selected articles from the first step by reviewing their full text. Any disagree - ments were discussed with a third author (KD) until consensus was reached.
